sections.title: Kelp Forest
sections.text:
Kelp Forest Exhibits EXHIBIT EXHIBIT_SPACE 1.2.3 2026-06-26 Guide-friendly companion page for the Monterey Bay Aquarium Kelp Forest exhibit, with quick facts, visitor Q&A, conservation messages, volunteer talking points, references, and troubleshooting support. Core update This version adds an easy close button to the Troubleshooting panel while preserving the top-bar controls. View into a kelp forest exhibit with kelp and fish MBA Naturalist Library image approved for internal volunteer Hub use. ~400 individual fish on exhibit, not counting schooling anchovies. About 42 fish species, 56 invertebrate species, and 67 algae species are represented in the exhibit census. The exhibit is about 31 feet deep total, with about 28 feet of water. The exhibit holds approximately 340,000 gallons, or about 1.26 million liters, of seawater. Water enters at about 1,600 gallons per minute, with a full turnover about every 2 to 2.5 hours. Typical exhibit temperature range: 48–58°F, or about 8.9–14.4°C. Kelp in the exhibit is commonly reported to grow about 4–5 inches per day. Feeding is usually once daily, often around 11:30 a.m. or 2:30 p.m.; exact timing can vary. Giant kelp can grow several inches in a single day. It makes an underwater forest where fish can hide, hunt, rest, and grow up. Look into the Kelp Forest and imagine swimming through a forest where the trees sway with the waves instead of the wind. Giant kelp forms the living structure, while fish, crabs, sea stars, anemones, urchins, and many other animals use different parts of the forest like rooms in a home.

This exhibit is one of the Aquarium’s signature achievements. Before the Aquarium opened in 1984, growing giant kelp successfully in an aquarium had not been done at this scale. The open top brings in sunlight, cold bay water brings nutrients, and the surge machine creates the back-and-forth motion kelp needs.

A good visitor message is simple: kelp forests are communities. When we protect the habitat, make smart seafood choices, and support healthy ocean management, the whole community has a better chance to thrive. Exhibit dimensions and systems The Kelp Forest exhibit is approximately 66 feet long by 28 feet wide, with a total depth of about 31 feet and about 28 feet of water. It holds approximately 340,000 gallons of seawater. Water turnover is commonly listed at about 1,600 gallons per minute, with a full turnover about every 2 to 2.5 hours. The first-floor windows are about 15 feet tall and 7.25 inches thick, weighing about 2.5 tons each. The rockwork is fiberglass-reinforced concrete, not real rock. How the kelp stays alive The exhibit is open to the sky so giant kelp can receive direct sunlight for photosynthesis. Cold, nutrient-rich seawater from Monterey Bay helps support kelp growth. A surge machine built into the left rockwork creates a standing wave, often described as about 12–14 inches, to mimic natural ocean surge and keep nutrients moving across the kelp. Animals on exhibit Commonly noted animals include northern anchovies, blue rockfish, blacksmith, gopher rockfish, striped seaperch, señorita, kelp surfperch, salema, halfmoon, opaleye, red sea urchin, copper rockfish, giant kelpfish, black rockfish, California sea cucumber, northern kelp crab, kelp greenling, California sheephead, kelp bass, bat stars, leopard sharks, wolf eels, giant sea bass, swell shark, and spiny lobster. Counts change over time, so use the current animal census for precise daily numbers. Fish ecology Kelp forests create many living spaces: canopy, midwater, rock faces, crevices, holdfasts, and the seafloor. Small schooling fish may use the forest as shelter. Rockfish, surfperch, kelpfish, and other species use the structure in different ways. Predators such as kelp bass, giant sea bass, leopard sharks, wolf eels, and larger rockfish help shape the community. Invertebrates and algae Invertebrates are a major part of the kelp forest community. Sea stars, anemones, crabs, sea cucumbers, urchins, chitons, limpets, and spiny lobsters all use the habitat. Some filter food from the water, some graze algae, some eat drifting kelp pieces, and some hunt or scavenge. Giant kelp, Macrocystis pyrifera, is the ecosystem engineer that creates much of the structure. Conservation messaging Kelp forests connect naturally to three visitor messages: protect habitat, choose seafood responsibly, and understand the value of marine protected areas. Rockfish recovery is a strong local story: many rockfish populations were hurt by overfishing, and better management helped many groundfish fisheries improve. Marine protected areas can work like a bank account for ocean life, allowing animals and habitats to recover and support surrounding waters. Spanish naming note The exhibit name in Spanish is Bosque de Macroalgas. The Spanish common name note from the source app says giant kelp should be referred to as macrocistis rather than the outdated cachiyuyo. Use current MBA Naturalist Library language standards when updating this page. How deep is the Kelp Forest tank? It is about 31 feet deep total, with about 28 feet of water. The first-floor windows are about 15 feet tall and over 7 inches thick. How much water does it hold? About 340,000 gallons, or roughly 1.26 million liters. Water is pumped in from Monterey Bay and turns over about every 2 to 2.5 hours. Are the rocks real? No. The rockwork is fiberglass-reinforced concrete. It is designed to look like natural rocky reef while staying strong and lightweight enough for the exhibit. How fast does kelp grow? In this exhibit, kelp is commonly reported to grow about 4–5 inches per day. Growth depends on light, nutrients, water motion, and conditions in the exhibit. Why is the exhibit open at the top? Giant kelp needs sunlight for photosynthesis, so the open top lets natural light reach the kelp. That is one of the features that helps this living forest grow indoors. What makes the wave? A surge machine built into the rockwork pushes water back and forth. That motion mimics natural ocean surge and helps move nutrients across the kelp. When is feeding? Feeding is usually once daily, often around 11:30 a.m. or 2:30 p.m., but times can vary. Check the day’s schedule before giving visitors a specific time. What do the animals eat? The exhibit diet may include items such as squid, shrimp or prawns, whitefish, sardines, and krill. Different animals feed in different ways, just as they would in a natural kelp forest food web. What is an MPA? An MPA is a Marine Protected Area. It is a place where some activities are limited so ocean life and habitats have room to recover and grow. Why are kelp forests important? They provide food, shelter, nursery space, and hunting grounds for many animals. They also help visitors see that a habitat is more than a backdrop — it is a living community. Start with what visitors can see: swaying kelp, schooling fish, rockfish holding still, sea stars on the windows, or the surge moving the whole forest. Helpful analogy: kelp is like the trees in a forest, but it is algae, not a plant. It creates structure that many animals use. Another analogy: MPAs can work like a bank account for ocean health — life grows inside and can help surrounding waters over time. Point out that the rocks are not real. This often surprises visitors and opens a conversation about exhibit design. For kids, invite them to look for camouflage: giant kelpfish can blend into kelp, while rockfish often hover near structure. For conservation, connect kelp forests to Seafood Watch: responsible seafood choices help people and ocean wildlife share healthy food webs. Common misunderstanding: kelp is not a tree and not a true plant. Giant kelp is a brown alga. Time-sensitive details such as animal counts, feeding schedules, exhibit updates, and Naturalist Library language guidance should be refreshed when the Library is updated.
